title: Asynchronous token commit protocol and slab scheduling experiments
content:
Summary

This doc captures a prototype and experiment log for two related ideas we prototyped in Jan-Feb 2025: an asynchronous token commit protocol that separates visibility from kernel completion, and a slab-based scheduler for batching and affinity to reduce preemption noise. The goal is to reduce tail latency for streaming responses while keeping partial-token semantics consistent and KV cache correctness intact.

Motivation

We observed two recurring problems when optimizing for low-latency streaming:
- Long-running kernels or large batches cause head-of-line blocking for unrelated requests.
- Emitting partial tokens early improves client perceived latency but makes rollback and consistent KV cache state harder when preemption happens.

Two axes to explore: change scheduling to reduce harmful preemption, and change commit semantics so partial output is safe to expose and rollback if needed. Slab scheduling groups coroutines to reduce cross-request interference. Async commit separates client-visible emission from durable kernel commit.

Design overview: async token commit protocol

Key concepts
- Emit token candidate: a decoded token piece produced by the kernel that is not yet durable.
- Visibility fence: a logical point at which the runtime can send the token to the client stream. Visibility can be speculative and is revocable.
- Hard commit: the kernel has advanced KV state and token sequence in device memory and the host has acknowledged durability; rollback is no longer possible.
- Soft commit: host-level acknowledgment that the token is in the host transmit queue but device KV is not yet durable. Soft commits can be rolled back by replaying generation from last hard commit.

Protocol flow (happy path)
1. Kernel produces token candidate and appends to slab local buffer.
2. Runtime evaluates emission policy and may decide to make token visible immediately by passing to the streaming writer with a soft commit marker.
3. A background commit task serializes slab buffers to host-side queues and initiates device-level ops that make KV updates durable.
4. When device ack is received, the runtime upgrades the token to hard commit and clears rollback window.
5. If preemption or an interrupt occurs before hard commit, scheduler may cancel kernel or preempt; runtime must decide whether to revoke visible soft tokens and either replay from last hard commit or continue with fallback model.

Visibility semantics required
- Client-stream must accept that revoked tokens can be followed by correction tokens or a special revocation message; we prefer correction tokens to avoid breaking streaming parsers.
- Emit with sequence ids and checkpoint ids so clients and downstream ops can reconcile.

Slab scheduling prototype

Rationale
- Many short requests interleave on the same GPU causing context switches and kernel preemption overhead.
- If we colocate related requests that share KV locality and similar horizon lengths, we can batch more effectively and avoid costly preemption.

Slab model
- Slab := a soft partition on the GPU where multiple requests with affinity are grouped. Each slab has its own mini-queue and commit pipeline.
- Slabs are sized by expected token horizon and memory footprints. We allow dynamic slab resizing via compaction.
- Within a slab, we use a round-robin micro-scheduler to keep latency bounded. Slabs are scheduled onto SMs with kernel affinity hints.

Interaction with async commit
- Each slab manages its own soft commit window. Hard commits are triggered per-slab to avoid global stalls.
- Cross-slab KV writes are serialized at a higher level to preserve KV consistency. Slab-local KV writes are committed faster.

KV cache considerations

Consistency model
- We keep a monotonic per-request checkpoint id. KV entries are tagged with the checkpoint at which they were written. On rollback, we revert to last stable checkpoint.
- Slab-local caching requires eviction coordination: when slabs are compacted or moved, we must coordinate write-backs.

Compaction and migration
- Prototype supports moving a request from slab A to slab B when load imbalance occurs. We snapshot slab-local KV deltas to host and rehydrate on target slab. Snapshot is async and may extend soft-commit window.

Experiments plan and results (prototype runs)

Setup
- Two RTX A100 nodes, single GPU each, runtime patched with slab scheduler and async commit.
- Mixed workload: 70% short chat-like queries (avg 16 tokens), 30% long completions (avg 128 tokens). Traffic replay from production trace week 2025-01-08.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 client-observed first-byte latency, tail token latency, extra tokens emitted due to revocation, KV rollback rate, throughput (tokens/s), and preemption counts.

Preliminary results (summary)
- Slab scheduling reduced p99 first-byte latency for short queries by 22% compared to FIFO scheduling. p50 unchanged.
- Async soft-commit reduced median perceived streaming latency by 15ms because many tokens could be visible before hard commit.
- Revocation incidence: approx 0.8% of streams experienced at least one soft-token revocation under a synthetic preemption spike. Of those, 60% were resolved by injecting correction tokens, 40% required replay causing an extra ~45ms tail penalty.
- Overall throughput same within noise. KV rollback events were low but non-zero during aggressive compaction tests.

Tradeoffs observed
- Complexity: async commits require more bookkeeping and clients must handle corrections; libraries need to be updated.
- Correctness edge cases: cross-slab KV interactions and race windows during compaction need careful serialization.
- UI/UX: for many use cases, small corrections are acceptable; for others (financial/legal) revocations are unacceptable so those routes must force hard commits before emission.

Config knobs proposed
- soft_commit_window_ms: time budget to wait for hard commit before revocation risk becomes unacceptable.
- slab_target_horizon_tokens: target average horizon for slab sizing.
- correction_mode: inject_corrections | inject_revocation_marker | disable_soft_emit per route.
- commit_parallelism: number of concurrent slab commit tasks.

Open questions / next steps
- Client SDK behavior: what is the least-surprising correction envelope for streaming APIs? Survey UX team and product.
- Formalize invariants for cross-slab KV writes and derive a simple protocol for dependency tracking.
- Should we expose soft vs hard commit metrics in Console? Customers will want visibility into revocation rate.
- Stress-tests for compaction: need a targeted test that forces slab migrations under KM churn and verifies no silent data loss.
- Can we use lightweight kernel-side checkpoints to shorten hard commit latency?

Action items
- Prototype 2: implement correction_mode inject_corrections and add visible sequence ids in stream payload (owner: Marcus Li, due 2025-02-25).
- Benchmark: run a 48h mixed-workload replay with slab sizing auto-tuner enabled (owner: Jonah Kim, start 2025-02-20).
- UX: draft streaming correction envelope and error codes for revocation (owner: Renee Alvarez, due 2025-02-28).

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally experimental. Look for holes in the KV cross-slab model and places where a simpler restriction (eg disable soft emit for routes with cross-shard writes) could win engineering time.
- Logs and raw traces for the prototype runs are in linked artifacts. See GH PR for patch details and microbench scripts.

Appendix: quick failure scenarios and mitigation

1) Kernel crashes after soft emit but before hard commit
- Mitigation: mark stream as possibly inconsistent, schedule replay from last hard commit, inject correction tokens with a special checkpoint header.

2) Slab compaction moved a request while commit in flight
- Mitigation: stall migration until commit ack or sink commit to host-side delta log before move.

3) Sudden capacity pressure causes wide revocations
- Mitigation: degrade to conservative mode: disable soft emits and favor small batch kernels for fast hard commits.

End of doc

Quick links: see linked PR for implementation diffs, and INF-3172 for the tracking epic.
